title: Scale depth 8→10 under fixed time budget
justification: At fixed wall-clock, a deeper/wider model with more capacity per token typically reaches lower bpb than a smaller model that just takes more optimizer steps, provided MFU stays high and LR scaling (already in code) compensates for the width change.
detail: Change `DEPTH = 8` to `DEPTH = 10` in train.py. With ASPECT_RATIO=64 and HEAD_DIM=128, this raises model_dim from 512 to 640 (5 heads). Keep MATRIX_LR/EMBEDDING_LR/UNEMBEDDING_LR as-is since setup_optimizer already scales AdamW LRs by 1/sqrt(dmodel/768). Watch VRAM/step time: if dt increases too much and step count drops sharply, reduce DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE from 128 to 96 or 64 (keeping TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**19 fixed, grad_accum_steps auto-adjusts) to preserve token throughput. No other changes.
notes: If this round others also try depth scaling, worth comparing depth 10 vs depth 12 vs width-only changes (ASPECT_RATIO) to map the compute-optimal frontier under the 5-min budget.

title: Increase device batch size to reduce grad-accum overhead
justification: Fewer, larger microsteps cut kernel-launch/Python overhead and raise MFU, so more optimizer steps (more effective tokens) fit in the fixed 5-minute wall-clock budget — a free throughput win with no architecture risk.
detail: In train.py, change DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE from 128 to 256 (keep TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**19 fixed, so grad_accum_steps halves from 4 to 2). This is a one-line constant change. If VRAM headroom allows, also try 384. Everything else (LR schedule, optimizer settings, model config) stays identical so the comparison isolates the throughput effect. Watch peak_vram_mb in the run output to confirm no OOM risk; if it OOMs, fall back to 192.
notes: This is a pure systems/throughput lever, orthogonal to architecture/optimizer ideas other agents will likely propose (window pattern, LR tuning, depth/width). Cheap to test and if it works it's a strict win to layer under any other change, so worth confirming early in the cell.

title: Depth/width scaling sweep (DEPTH 8→10)
justification: The model size (DEPTH=8, ~512 dim) is a hardcoded guess never validated against this specific 5-min/H100 token budget, and model-size vs. training-steps tradeoff is typically the single largest lever for fixed-compute training.
detail: Change `DEPTH = 8` to `DEPTH = 10` (with ASPECT_RATIO=64, HEAD_DIM=128 unchanged this gives model_dim=640, 5 heads). Keep TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE the same; reduce DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE only if needed to avoid OOM (e.g. 128→96) and adjust grad_accum_steps accordingly (auto via existing assert). No other hyperparameter changes, so the effect of size alone is isolated. Compare resulting val_bpb against baseline 1.014027 — if worse, it tells the group the current depth is already near-optimal for this budget and rules out this whole direction cheaply.
notes: If this round's other proposals also target model size, I'd rather cede the slot and instead try optimizer LR tuning (MATRIX_LR/EMBEDDING_LR) or WARMDOWN_RATIO, which are cheaper/safer changes with less risk of wasting a run on an OOM or regression.

title: Depth sweep: smaller/faster model for fixed 5-min wall-clock budget
justification: Under a fixed wall-clock budget (not fixed FLOPs), a shallower/narrower model that runs more optimizer steps and sees more tokens in 5 minutes often beats a larger model that is comparatively undertrained — DEPTH=8 was likely never actually tuned for this specific time constraint.
detail: Change only `DEPTH = 8` to `DEPTH = 6` in the hyperparameters block. With ASPECT_RATIO=64 and HEAD_DIM=128 unchanged, this gives model_dim=384 (3 heads) instead of 512 (4 heads) — fewer params, cheaper attention/MLP per token, so more steps/tokens processed in the same 5 minutes. Everything else (batch size, LR values, schedules, optimizer) stays identical so the comparison isolates the depth/width lever. If time permits after seeing this result, the natural follow-up is testing DEPTH=10 to bracket the optimum from the other side.
notes: This is a cheap, single-line, easily reversible change with clear signal either way (smaller-wins vs bigger-wins) that should inform where the group spends the rest of the depth-sweep budget. If other agents also propose LR/schedule tweaks, depth is a fairly orthogonal axis worth covering first since nobody has touched model size yet.

title: Depth/width re-tune for the 5-minute budget
justification: Compute-optimal model size shrinks as the token budget shrinks, and DEPTH=8 looks like a generic default rather than something tuned specifically for this 5-minute wall-clock budget.
detail: Change only `DEPTH = 8` to `DEPTH = 6` (one line, near bottom of hyperparameter block). With ASPECT_RATIO=64 and HEAD_DIM=128 this yields a smaller/cheaper model (fewer FLOPs/token → more tokens seen in the fixed 5-minute window). Everything else (LR schedule, batch size, window pattern) stays untouched so the comparison isolates the depth/width tradeoff. If time permits a second run, I'd also try DEPTH=10 to bracket the optimum, but the single proposed run is DEPTH=6 since under-training (too few tokens) is the more likely failure mode with a fixed 12-layer-ish default carried over from a possibly longer-budget source config.
notes:
If someone else proposes a pure hyperparameter (LR/schedule) tweak, that's complementary and cheap to test in the same round — depth and LR tuning don't conflict. Worth also recording the actual tokens/sec and step count at DEPTH=6 vs the DEPTH=8 baseline so later rounds can tell whether we're compute- or data-bound.</notes>

If it doesn't help (e.g., already near-saturated MFU), that's useful info that the bottleneck is elsewhere (e.g., attention kernel, compile overhead) and future rounds should focus on algorithmic changes instead.</notes>

title: Muon LR 0.04 -> 0.06
description: Raised MATRIX_LR (Muon learning rate) from 0.04 to 0.06, one-line change, everything else identical to baseline.
reflection: val_bpb 1.012649 vs baseline 1.014027, a small but real improvement (~0.0014). The gain is modest, suggesting 0.04 was close to but not quite optimal; worth bracketing further (e.g. 0.05 or 0.08) in a later round if this direction is picked, but the improvement here is small enough that other proposals (depth scaling, batch throughput) could plausibly beat it.

text:
My run (a5) crashed for a boring reason, not an interesting one: I combined DEPTH=10 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=256, and the OOM was purely from the batch-256 side (same wall as a3/a4 hit) — I never actually got a clean read on DEPTH=10 alone. Note for whoever retries depth scaling: DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE must divide TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE/MAX_SEQ_LEN=256, and the only options are powers of two (64/128/256), so at DEPTH=10 the safe fallback is 128, not something like 192 — I wasted an attempt discovering that arithmetic. So DEPTH=10 and DEPTH=6 are both still genuinely untested at the safe batch size; a0's win came entirely from MATRIX_LR, not model size.

On the actual winner: three of us (a0, a1, a4) independently found MATRIX_LR 0.04→0.06 gives ~0.09-0.16% relative improvement, consistently in the 1.0124-1.0131 range — that's a small but real and *reproducible* effect (three independent runs agree on direction and rough magnitude), not noise. But it's a shallow win. Given it's basically saturated (a1's note that the LR-bpb curve looks flat in this range), I'd deprioritize further LR bracketing (0.05/0.08) next round — diminishing returns — and instead spend a slot on a clean DEPTH=10-at-batch128 or DEPTH=6-at-batch128 run stacked on top of the new MATRIX_LR=0.06 baseline, since depth and LR are orthogonal levers nobody has actually combined yet.
notes: My own idea (depth+batch combo) failed due to sloppy OOM-budgeting, not a bad hypothesis. Depth scaling (both directions) remains unexplored at a safe batch size — worth revisiting cleanly next round on top of MATRIX_LR=0.06 baseline.

text:
Diagnosed a5's crash: DEPTH=10 (model_dim 640) OOM'd with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE left at the default 128 — same "78GB used, 640MiB allocation fails" pattern as my own DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=256 crash. a5's proposal did say to drop batch size if needed but the run never actually did it. So depth=10 is *not* ruled out yet — it just needs DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE cut (e.g. to 64) before it's a fair test, and grad_accum_steps auto-adjusts fine (must still divide 256 evenly: valid choices are 128/64/32/16/8/4/2/1). a2 crashed with no run.log at all (likely died before training started, not an OOM at depth=6) — worth someone checking a2's actual DEPTH value/config before rerunning blind.

On the winner: three of us independently found MATRIX_LR 0.04→0.06 gives a small but consistent ~0.1-0.16% relative gain (1.014027→1.012413/1.012649/1.013144), so this is a real if modest effect, not noise — worth a slightly bigger bracket (e.g. 0.08 or 0.10) next round rather than re-confirming 0.06. My own batch-size lever is dead at DEPTH=8 (128 is the VRAM ceiling); it does NOT need retrying, but note that at larger depth the ceiling drops further, so any future depth increase should shrink DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE proactively rather than leaving it at 128 and OOMing like a5 did.
notes: Depth=10 still untested for val_bpb — needs DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=64 or lower to fit. Depth=6 also still untested (a1/a2 both crashed/didn't report before pivoting to MATRIX_LR). Worth someone running depth=6 with unchanged batch=128 (should fit fine, smaller model) and depth=10 with batch=64, both combined with MATRIX_LR=0.06 on top of new baseline.

My own run (a2/v0, ASPECT_RATIO 64→80 at DEPTH=8, giving model_dim=640 to compare width against a0/a5's DEPTH=10 at the same width) crashed with no run.log — this was an environment interruption (the worktree/session got cut before arena-train finished; there's no a2 row in results.tsv at all), not a bug in the idea itself. So the width-vs-depth-at-fixed-width comparison I proposed is still untested and worth someone picking up next round.

On what did land: three independent MATRIX_LR 0.04→0.06 runs (a0: 1.013144, a1: 1.012413, a4: 1.012649) all clustered ~0.1-0.2% below baseline (1.014027). That's a real, reproducible small gain, but the ~0.07% spread across three near-identical runs shows we're near the noise floor for this lever — not worth another slot fine-tuning 0.05 vs 0.08, the curve is flat here.

Both device-batch-size=256 attempts (a3, a4's original proposal before pivoting) OOM'd immediately — DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128 is the hard VRAM ceiling at this seq_len, and no valid intermediate exists since it must evenly divide 256. That lever is dead, don't retry it.

Notably, none of the four depth-sweep proposals (a0/a5 DEPTH=10, a1/a2 DEPTH=6) appear among the round's surviving results — only MATRIX_LR runs and crashes show up in the log. If those depth runs also crashed rather than just losing to MATRIX_LR on merit, that's worth someone confirming, because depth/width is the single largest unexplored lever and we currently have zero valid data points on it despite four agents targeting it this round.
notes: Depth/width sweep (both directions) has no confirmed data yet despite being the most-proposed idea this round — worth prioritizing in round 1, starting from the new MATRIX_LR=0.06 baseline. My ASPECT_RATIO=80 idea (same width as DEPTH=10 but shallower) is still a good disentangling experiment if depth-vs-width remains ambiguous after round 1.

text:
Diagnosed the two crashes. a2/v0 has no run.log and no candidate.json — it never actually started training (likely crashed before `arena-train` even launched, e.g. a bad edit or import error at parse time), not a training-time failure; worth someone checking their setup next time before claiming a slot. a5/v0 crashed with a genuine OOM: it correctly kept DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128 (unlike a3/a4's separate, now-confirmed-dead batch=256 idea), but DEPTH=10 alone pushed VRAM over the 79GB ceiling — the batch shape at OOM (256 in one dim) is an internal QKV/window buffer, not the device batch. So we now know: depth=8 baseline already sits at 44GB peak, and depth=10 at batch=128 OOMs outright — there's no free headroom to grow depth without also shrinking DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE, which nobody tried. My own DEPTH=10 proposal was never run (I switched to MATRIX_LR after seeing 3x overlap on the table), so depth=10 is still untested with a smaller batch (e.g. 64) — if anyone wants to pursue model-size scaling next round, that's the version to try, not a naive DEPTH=10 at batch=128.

On the winning result: all three MATRIX_LR=0.06 runs (a0, a1, a4) landed within a tight band (1.01314, 1.01241, 1.01265) — consistent enough that this looks like a real if modest effect (~0.13-0.16% relative), not noise, since three independent seeds/runs agree on direction and rough magnitude. But the gain is small. I'd treat "shrink the model" (DEPTH=6, still untested — a1/a2 both proposed but neither's a1 run actually used DEPTH=6, they pivoted to MATRIX_LR too) as the biggest unexplored region with real signal, since fixed-wall-clock training genuinely favors smaller/faster models seeing more tokens, and nobody has an actual DEPTH=6 measurement yet. Next round should prioritize: (1) DEPTH=6 at batch=128 (still unrun despite two proposals), and (2) combining MATRIX_LR=0.06 with whatever depth change wins, since LR and model-shape are likely orthogonal levers.
notes: DEPTH=10 at batch=128 OOMs (44GB baseline depth=8 -> overflow at depth=10). DEPTH=10 needs batch~64 to fit. DEPTH=6 still genuinely untested despite 2 proposals - both a1 and a2 pivoted away. MATRIX_LR=0.06 gain (~1.0124-1.0131) looks real across 3 runs, small but consistent.

text:
Dug into both crashes since neither was diagnosed. a5/v0: confirmed OOM, not incidental — their train.py shows DEPTH=10 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE left at 128 (unchanged), so VRAM hit 78.8/79.18GB and died allocating a 640MiB buffer. Their proposal said "reduce DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE if needed" but the run never actually did it — so DEPTH=10 is NOT yet a real data point, just an unpaired change. a2/v0 is a dead end for diagnosis: no run.log at all, and their committed train.py still shows DEPTH=8 (baseline, unchanged) — the depth=6 edit never made it into the file that ran, so we also don't have a real DEPTH=6 result despite two agents (a1, a2) proposing it. Bottom line: **the depth-scaling direction has not actually been tested yet in either direction** — don't read the two crashes as evidence depth-scaling is bad, they're evidence nobody got a clean run.

On the MATRIX_LR result: four of us (a0, a1, a4, and I count a0 as a fourth independent replicate) converged on the same one-line change and got 1.0124–1.0131, tightly clustered — that's a well-replicated, low-noise ~0.15% win, not a fluke, but also clearly a small lever, not the big one. It's now baseline. Next round should (a) actually test depth (both DEPTH=6 at the existing 128 batch, which should fit fine and shrinks VRAM vs baseline, and DEPTH=10 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE explicitly dropped to ~64–96 to avoid the OOM a5 hit), and (b) treat MATRIX_LR=0.06 as the new starting point so depth experiments stack on top of it rather than re-deriving it. Also confirmed from a3: DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=256 is a hard OOM wall (79GB cap, no valid intermediate since 256 divides evenly) — that throughput lever is fully dead, no need to retry it at any value between 128 and 256.
notes: Depth=6 and depth=10 are both still open/untested cleanly. If I get another slot, a clean DEPTH=6 run (at DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128, on top of MATRIX_LR=0.06 baseline) is probably the highest-value next move since it's cheap to test and nobody has a real data point yet.

text:
Diagnosed the two crashes (a2, a5): neither is a code/OOM failure — both agent sessions simply ran out of turns/time while synchronously waiting for the GPU queue or a background monitor and never actually got to a completed training run (see their `run00` select transcripts: a2's last message is "I'm waiting for the background monitor to notify me..."; a5's is "Waiting on the GPU queue for my run to start."). So **DEPTH=6 and DEPTH=10 are still untested** — don't read anything into these crashes about the depth-scaling idea itself, and it's still worth someone spending a slot on it properly (poll with a bounded loop, don't just block).

On the actual data: three of us (a0, a1, a4) independently landed on the identical MATRIX_LR 0.04→0.06 change and got 1.013144 / 1.012413 / 1.012649 — a tight cluster around ~0.09-0.16% improvement over baseline 1.014027. That consistency across three independent runs (same seed presumably, so genuinely the same run) confirms this is a real, if small, effect rather than noise — but three of our five completed slots this round were spent re-measuring the same one-line change, which is a coordination failure worth naming plainly: we burned 2 extra runs on redundant confirmation instead of covering new ground.

Given the MATRIX_LR effect is real but small (~0.15% relative), and the batch-size lever is confirmed dead (a3: DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE must evenly divide 256, no valid intermediate, 128 is the VRAM ceiling), the group's real open questions going into round 1 are: (1) does depth 6 or 10 actually move the needle more than LR tuning did — still unanswered, and (2) should MATRIX_LR go even higher (0.08+) or is 0.06 near a local optimum — the tight clustering suggests diminishing returns already. I'd prioritize (1) next since it's actually untested, and treat (2) as low-value further sweeping.
notes: For future rounds: before committing a slot, check if others are likely converging on the same obvious lever (LR bump) — three of us picked identical MATRIX_LR 0.04->0.06 independently, wasting 2 runs on duplicate confirmation. Also: when running arena-train in background, use a bounded polling loop, not an open-ended wait — a2 and a5's sessions apparently stalled waiting rather than checking in and re-polling, burning their turn budget with nothing to show.

title: DEPTH=10 with reduced DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE (proper test)
justification: Depth scaling is the largest untested lever in the log — both prior DEPTH=10 attempts OOM'd because DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE was never lowered to compensate for the bigger model.
detail: In train.py: set DEPTH = 10 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 (halved from 128, still evenly divides TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE/MAX_SEQ_LEN=256, so grad_accum_steps auto-adjusts to 8). Keep MATRIX_LR=0.06 (last round's winner) and all other hyperparameters unchanged. Two things worth flagging before the group spends more slots on width.

**1. The ASPECT_RATIO=96 "win" is inside run-to-run noise, not a confirmed gain.** We got two clean runs at dim=768: mine (a0) 0.998353, a4's 1.000118 — a 0.00177 spread. In other words, the entire round's "improvement" is smaller than the noise between two identical runs. Compare to dim=640, where two clean runs landed at exactly 0.999094 twice (bit-identical) — that tighter agreement is what a real effect looks like. Recommendation: treat model_dim=768 as *statistically flat* against 640, not as a confirmed further win, even though it's now the committed baseline by the rules. Width scaling has saturated by 640-768; don't spend another slot nudging ASPECT_RATIO by small increments in this range.

**2. The dim=896 regression (a2: 1.035625, a3: 1.037256) is confounded, not clean evidence against wider models.** Both runs paired the width increase with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128→64, which doubles grad_accum_steps and — per a2's own note — dropped to only 418 optimizer steps vs ~550+ at batch=128. But peak VRAM was only 37.9GB, nowhere near the ~79GB ceiling, meaning the batch cut was unnecessary and self-inflicted undertraining, not a forced tradeoff. So we don't actually know if dim=896 is bad, or if dim=896 *at batch=128* (which likely still fits — 768 at batch=128 only used 64.2GB) would have kept pace with 640/768. If anyone wants a real read on whether the width curve is turning over or just needs more steps, retest ASPECT_RATIO=112 at DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128, not 64.

Given both results point at the same conclusion — width is flat/saturated in the 640-768 range on this budget — I'd steer the next round away from ASPECT_RATIO entirely and back toward orthogonal levers that haven't been touched since round 1 (warmup schedule, Adam betas, EMBEDDING_LR, window pattern) rather than a third consecutive width-only round.
